course: NISM Series XIII: Common Derivatives Certification Examination
overview: This chapter explains how to record your trading profits/losses in your account books (Accounting) and how the government taxes them (Taxation). This is often confusing because the English meaning of 'Speculation' is different from the Income Tax meaning. The most important exam question here is whether F&O trading is 'Speculative Business' or 'Non-Speculative Business'.

complete_concept_explanation.concept: 1. Classification of Income (Business vs Capital Gain)
complete_concept_explanation.basic_meaning: How does the Income Tax Department view your trading? Is it a Business or an Investment?
complete_concept_explanation.detailed_explanation:
For most traders and exam purposes, F&O trading is treated as **Business Income**, not Capital Gains.

**Why?**
Because derivatives have a short life (max 3 months) and are usually traded frequently for profit, not held for years like an investment.

**Therefore:**
* You must report it under the head **'Profits and Gains of Business or Profession' (PGBP)**.
* You can deduct expenses (Internet bill, advisory fees, books, depreciation on computer) from your profit to lower your tax.
complete_concept_explanation.why_this_is_important: Exam asks: 'Under which head is F&O income taxed?' Answer: Business Income.
complete_concept_explanation.formula: Taxable Income = Total F&O Profit - Valid Business Expenses
complete_concept_explanation.formula_explanation: You pay tax only on the net profit.
complete_concept_explanation.step_by_step_calculation_example:
**Scenario:**
Gross F&O Profit = ₹5,00,000.
Brokerage Paid = ₹50,000.
Internet/Software Cost = ₹20,000.

**Calculation:**
Net Business Income = $5,00,000 - 50,000 - 20,000 = \text{₹4,30,000}$.
You pay tax on ₹4.3 Lakhs.
complete_concept_explanation.real_life_indian_example: A full-time trader in Delhi files **ITR-3** (Income Tax Return for Business) and shows his trading profits as business income, allowing him to claim a deduction for his laptop purchase.
exam_traps: Thinking F&O is Capital Gains. (It is rarely Capital Gains, usually Business Income).
Thinking you cannot deduct expenses. (Since it is Business, you CAN deduct expenses).

complete_concept_explanation.concept: 2. Speculative vs. Non-Speculative Business (The Big Twist)
complete_concept_explanation.basic_meaning: Is F&O trading considered 'Speculation' by Tax Law? Surprisingly, NO.
complete_concept_explanation.detailed_explanation:
This is the most critical concept.

**Section 43(5) of Income Tax Act:**
1.  **Speculative Transaction:** A transaction settled **without** actual delivery. (e.g., Intraday Equity Trading).
2.  **Exception (The Twist):** Derivatives (Futures & Options) traded on a **Recognized Stock Exchange (like NSE/BSE)** are **NOT** treated as Speculative Transactions.

**Conclusion:** Exchange Traded F&O is **Non-Speculative Business Income** (also called 'Normal Business Income').
complete_concept_explanation.why_this_is_important: If it is 'Non-Speculative', you can set off losses against other income (like Salary or Rental income), which is a huge tax benefit. 'Speculative' losses cannot be set off easily.
complete_concept_explanation.real_life_indian_example:
Rahul makes a loss of ₹1 Lakh in F&O. He earns ₹5 Lakhs from a Shoe Shop (Normal Business). 
Since F&O is also 'Normal Business', he can subtract the loss: $5L - 1L = 4L$. He pays tax only on 4L.
exam_traps: Thinking F&O is Speculative because it involves risk. (In English yes, in Tax Law NO).
complete_concept_explanation.memory_trick: Exchange Traded = Digital Proof = Not Gambling = Non-Speculative.

complete_concept_explanation.basic_meaning: A direct tax collected by the exchange on every trade you do.
complete_concept_explanation.detailed_explanation:
You pay this tax automatically when you trade. It is collected by the broker and given to the government.

**Rules:**
1.  **Futures:** Paid on **Sell** side only.
2.  **Options:** Paid on **Sell** side (on Premium). Also paid on **Exercise** (on Settlement Price) if you hold ITM till expiry.
3.  **Deduction:** Since F&O is a business, STT paid is allowed as a **Business Expense** (you can subtract it from profit).
complete_concept_explanation.why_this_is_important: Exam often asks: 'Is STT deductible?' Yes, if it is Business Income.
complete_concept_explanation.real_life_indian_example: Check your 'Contract Note' from Zerodha/Upstox. You will see a small amount deducted as STT on every sell order.
exam_traps: Thinking STT is paid on Buy side for F&O. (Usually Sell side only).
Thinking STT cannot be claimed as expense. (For Business Income, it is deductible).
complete_concept_explanation.memory_trick: STT = Sell Transaction Tax (Mostly on Sell).

complete_concept_explanation.basic_meaning: How to write these trades in your accounting books (Balance Sheet/P&L).
complete_concept_explanation.detailed_explanation:
The Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI) mandates that you must recognize losses immediately.

**Prudence Principle:**
* If you have an open position at the end of the year (31st March) and it is in **Loss**, you MUST record that loss in P&L immediately (provide for it).
* If it is in **Profit**, you generally ignore it until you actually book it (Conservative approach), although MTM accounting often requires recording fair value changes.
complete_concept_explanation.real_life_indian_example: A company holds Nifty Futures on 31st March with a paper loss of ₹10 Lakhs. Even though they haven't sold it yet, their Balance Sheet must show this ₹10 Lakh liability.
exam_traps: Thinking you only record loss when you sell. (No, Mark-to-Market losses must be provided for at year-end).
complete_concept_explanation.memory_trick: Losses = Shout loud (Record now). Profits = Keep quiet (Record later).

important_differences.clear_explanation:
1. **Speculative:** Intraday Equity Trading. Losses can ONLY be set off against Speculative Profits. (Cannot deduct from Salary/Other Business).
2. **Non-Speculative:** F&O Trading. Losses can be set off against ANY Business Income (except Salary). Loss can be carried forward for 8 years.

1. **Business Income:** Trading is your profession/business. STT is deductible. Taxed at slab rates (up to 30%).
2. **Capital Gains:** Investing for long term. STT is NOT deductible. Taxed at special rates (15% or 10%).

frequently_asked_exam_areas: Is F&O trading Speculative or Non-Speculative? (Answer: Non-Speculative Business).
Can STT be claimed as a business expense? (Answer: Yes).
On which side is STT usually charged in Futures? (Answer: Sell side).
Which section of Income Tax Act defines Speculative Transactions? (Answer: Section 43(5)).
quick_revision_summary: STT is paid on Sell side for Futures/Options.
STT is a valid business expense (deductible).
Losses in F&O can be set off against other business profits.
Account books must record MTM losses at year-end (Prudence).
